title: The hard century close
hookLine: from Banda to Lahore: the hard century remembered in every Ardas

cards: Weeks ago on this path, a Guru at Nanded met an ascetic who became Banda, the servant, and rode north with five arrows.

Since then: towns taken and lost, a siege in a mud fort, a march to Delhi, a scholar executed for a festival, a humble nawab, forests and deserts, two holocausts, a temple blown up and rebuilt, Sirhind, and chiefs riding into Lahore.
A long road. And all of it, Sikhs say, is folded into a few lines they say standing. Today: the hard century close.

teach.h: THE CENTURY FOLDED INTO THE PRAYER.
teach.b: Go back to the Ardas passage you met a few days ago.

It remembers Sikhs cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, who gave their heads but kept their faith, who kept their hair to the last breath, who gave their lives for the gurdwaras. The prayer doesn't name them.
But Sikhs listening hear particular people. Tradition links cut limb from limb to Bhai Mani Singh, whom you met at the Diwali gathering.
Broken on the wheel calls up the father and son, Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh. Scalped calls up Bhai Taru Singh, who, tradition says, gave up his scalp rather than his hair.
So much of the century you just walked through is inside the prayer. Second, who says it. Not historians first.
A grandmother at dawn. A child at a school assembly. A family before a long drive.

The hard century is kept in the mouths of ordinary people, standing, hands folded. Third, the tone. The passage remembers what was endured, then the Ardas moves on to ask for the Name, for humility, for the good of all.

teach.h: MEMORY, ASKING, THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: Memory, then asking, then a wish for everyone. That's the shape these weeks have followed: the servant and his arrows, the hunted years, the ruins, the turn, and a people still singing at the end.
All that story lives in a prayer said standing.

how: Sikhs say the Ardas standing at the close of prayers and gatherings, and its martyrs' passage remembers by their deeds the Sikhs of the persecutions; the congregation answers Waheguru after it.

games.q: you want a hunted century remembered by ordinary families, every day, long after the last rider dies. where do you put it?
o: in a chronicle kept in a library.
in a few lines of the prayer everyone says standing.
on a monument in the capital.
games.why: Sikhs carry it in the martyrs' passage of the Ardas. a grandmother at dawn says it as surely as any historian.

practice: If you pray the Ardas, stand, fold your hands, and say the martyrs' passage slowly, letting each line call up a face from these weeks.
If you don't, sit and let the lines come back, cut limb from limb, broken on the wheel, scalped, with a breath after each for someone who stood. End with one breath for the good of all.

wordCard.voice: Ardas, the standing prayer whose martyrs' passage, Sikhs say, folds in the whole century: from Banda's five arrows to chiefs in Lahore. Today's word.
